content: Early pregnancy factor (EPF), also known as early conception factor (ECF), is a protein associated with mammalian embryos shortly after fertilization. It may consist of more than one molecular component. EPF was first identified in 1976. EPF can be detected using the rosette inhibition test. This protein is present in maternal serum (blood plasma) shortly after fertilization and can also be found in cervical mucus and amniotic fluid. In sheep, EPF can be detected within 72 hours of mating, while in mice, it is detectable within 24 hours. In humans, EPF has been identified in the media surrounding embryos fertilized in vitro within 48 hours of fertilization, although some studies have failed to replicate this finding. EPF has been detected as early as six hours after mating in some cases. However, the rosette inhibition test is an indirect method, and substances with similar effects can interfere with the results. For example, pig semen has been shown to inhibit rosette formation, leading to a positive test result in sows mated with vasectomized boars, but not in those exposed to similar stimulation without semen. Despite initial challenges in consistently detecting EPF in post-conception females, its existence is now widely accepted in the scientific community, and progress has been made in characterizing this protein. EPF is not believed to be directly produced by early embryos. Instead, embryos likely produce a chemical signal that induces the maternal system to generate EPF. After implantation, the conceptus itself may produce EPF. This protein functions as an immunosuppressant and, along with other substances associated with early embryos, is thought to help prevent the maternal immune system from attacking the embryo. Experiments in mice have shown that injecting anti-EPF antibodies after mating significantly reduces the number of successful pregnancies and offspring. However, when embryos were cultured in media containing anti-EPF antibodies, no effect on growth was observed. While some actions of EPF, such as rosette inhibition, are consistent across mammalian species, other immunosuppressive mechanisms vary. In mice, EPF levels are high during early pregnancy but decline to non-pregnant levels by day 15. In humans, EPF levels remain elevated for the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, then decrease and become undetectable within eight weeks after delivery. Recent research suggests that EPF may also play a role in cell proliferation in various biological contexts beyond embryonic development. In 1979, it was proposed that EPF could serve as a marker for very early pregnancy testing and for monitoring the viability of ongoing pregnancies in livestock. Interest in this application has persisted, but current testing methods have not proven accurate enough for practical use in livestock management. In humans, modern pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is only present after implantation, occurring six to twelve days after fertilization. In contrast, EPF is detectable within hours of fertilization, making it the earliest known marker of pregnancy. Although other pre-implantation signals have been identified, EPF remains the most promising early marker. Studies have found EPF to be highly accurate as a pregnancy test in humans. EPF may also be useful in research on birth control mechanisms. It can help determine whether contraceptive methods act before or after fertilization. For example, a study on women using intrauterine devices (IUDs) found that post-fertilization mechanisms significantly contribute to their effectiveness. For groups that define pregnancy as beginning at fertilization, contraceptives with post-fertilization effects are considered abortifacient. There is ongoing debate about whether hormonal contraceptives, particularly the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), have post-fertilization effects. The organization Pharmacists for Life has called for large-scale clinical trials to evaluate EPF levels in women using COCPs, which could provide definitive evidence on this issue. EPF is also valuable in studying infertility and early pregnancy loss. It can help distinguish between infertility caused by failure to conceive and infertility caused by failure to implant. In one study of healthy women trying to conceive, EPF detected 14 pregnancies, six of which were lost within ten days of ovulation, indicating a 43% rate of early conceptus loss. EPF has been proposed as a marker for viable pregnancies, potentially more effective than hCG or progesterone in identifying ectopic or nonviable pregnancies. In women treated with clomiphene for infertility, fertilization rates per cycle were approximately 40%-50%. However, in cycles where fertilization occurred, nearly 80% of pregnancies resulted in subclinical embryonic loss, a much higher rate than in healthy women. In vitro fertilization (IVF) studies have shown that while many embryos fail to implant, a significant number are likely damaged or killed during the transfer process. These findings highlight the need for improved embryo transfer techniques in IVF. Although EPF is primarily associated with pregnancy, EPF-like activity has also been detected in tumors, particularly those of germ cell origin, as well as in other types of tumors. Its potential use as a tumor marker has been suggested, particularly for evaluating the success of surgical treatments.
